COMMENT: in Otetela there are a few cases of long vowels, but this always seems to be through consonant elision and vowel assimilation ... 10. Stress (accent of intensity) on the syllable of the radical (as in Zone B). 11. Lexical tone on the radical as well as on the suffixes.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Files checked under (directory exists with even though our source list 'held' is empty). (1) Labaere 2001, lines 6165-6176: '9. Une seule more (quantite) seulement sur la voyelle de radicaux. (De meme dans les Zones A,B,D.) / COMMENTAIRE En ttla il y a quelques cas de voyelle longue, mais ce semble etre toujours par elision de consonne et assimilation vocalique.. / 10. Accent d'intensite sur la syllabe du radical (Ainsi en Zone B.) / 11. Ton lexical tant sur le radical que sur les suffixes. (Ainsi en Zones B,D,L)'. Matches the reported quote; only differences are stripped diacritics, the compiler '[..]' elisions, and 'otetela' where the text has 'ttla' (the PDF text drops the open-vowel let…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand only: Guthrie's zone-level generalization, reproduced for Tetela by the Tetela grammarian Labaere without objection, places dynamic stress on the (first) syllable of the radical, i.e. stem-initial; Hyman 2009 likewise lists Tetela among NW Bantu languages with (stem-)initial prominence. All first-hand descriptions opened (Jacobs 1962, Daeleman 1982, Labaere 1987, Wetshemongo 2020) describe Tetela as a two-tone language (H vs L, tone-bearing geminate consonants, H-tone spread) and say nothing about stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Labaere adds no Tetela-specific remark to Guthrie's stress item, whereas he corrects Guthrie elsewhere (vowel system, length, tone).
new_statements.domain_note: Stem/radical-anchored (morphological) position per Guthrie's formulation; Hyman notes 'initial' in NW Bantu usually means stem-initial. Tetela is lexically tonal (two tonemes; Jacobs 1962:32, saved file line 58), so any stress is non-contrastive and co-exists with tone.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern Tetela proper (tete1250, C71); Jacobs 1962 and Labaere describe the central norm (Mondja/Tshumbe and Ewango/Wembo-Nyama dialects). Related but distinct varieties encountered: Lonkutsu/Nkutsu C73 (Motingea 1989; nkut1238) and Otetela-Hamba of Lomela (Kasongo 1993; Glottolog hamb1245), neither with a stress statement.

sources.citation: Labaere, R. 1987. La consonne geminee en tetela (Zaire). Annales Aequatoria 8: 349-354.
sources.note: Geminate consonant = realization of mora+tone of a reduced first-degree vowel; geminate is syllabic and tone-bearing; progressive tonal assimilation. No stress/accent statement.

sources.citation: Jacobs, John. 1962. De belangrijkste elementen van het Tetela-toonsysteem (Kasayi-Kivu, Congo). Africana Linguistica 1: 31-42. DOI 10.3406/aflin.1962.856 (Persee).
sources.note: Purely tonal description: 'Het Tetela beschikt over twee tonemen: een gelijkmatig hoog en een gelijkmatig laag toneem', borne by vowels and by long consonants; compound (falling/rising) tones on vowels; simple nasals toneless. No mention of stress/accent (klemtoon, nadruk, intensiteit) anywhere in the 12 pages.

tone.quote: De linguistische basis van het signaaltrommel-prineipe is vol- doende gekend. We handelen hier ook niet in bijzonderheden over de verhouding tussen de plaatselijk gesproken taal en de signaal- trommeltaal. Zoals bekend worden de tonen van het woord dat men wil mededelen, op het instrument weergegeven. Daar nu onein- dig veel woorden dezelfde tonen hebben en om verwarring uit te sluiten, zal de trommelaar het denkbeeld dat hij wil overseinen „uitbreiden”.
tone.translation: The linguistic basis of the signal-drum principle is sufficiently known. We also do not deal here in detail with the relation between the locally spoken language and the signal-drum language. As is known, the tones of the word one wants to communicate are reproduced on the instrument. Since infinitely many words have the same tones, and to exclude confusion, the drummer will 'expand' the idea he wants to transmit.
tone.summary: Tone is presupposed, not described: the tones of a word are reproduced on the slit drum and many words share the same tones; c. 110 drum phrases printed with tone marks; no inventory or analysis.
